{{Short description|In statistics, a measurement of the agreement between two variables}}
In [[statistics]], the '''concordance correlation coefficient''' measures the agreement between two variables, e.g., to evaluate [[reproducibility]] or for [[inter-rater reliability]].

==Definition==
The form of the concordance correlation coefficient <math>\rho_c</math> as<ref name="LinL1989Concordance">{{Cite journal
 | author = Lawrence I-Kuei Lin |author1-link=Lawrence I-Kuei Lin
 | title = A concordance correlation coefficient to evaluate reproducibility
 | journal = [[Biometrics (journal)|Biometrics]]
 | volume = 45
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 255&ndash;268
 |date=March 1989
 | pmid = 2720055
 | doi = 10.2307/2532051
 | jstor = 2532051
 }}</ref>
:<math>\rho_c = \frac{2\rho\sigma_x\sigma_y}{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + (\mu_x - \mu_y)^2},</math>
where <math>\mu_x</math> and <math>\mu_y</math> are the [[mean]]s for the two variables and <math>\sigma^2_x</math> and <math>\sigma^2_y</math> are the corresponding [[variance]]s. <math>\rho</math> is [[Pearson correlation coefficient|Pearson's correlation coefficient]] between the two variables.

This follows from its definition<ref name="LinL1989Concordance"/>, as:
:<math>\rho_c = 1 - \frac{{\rm Expected\ orthogonal\ squared\ distance\ from\ the\ diagonal\ }x=y}
{{\rm Expected\ orthogonal\ squared\ distance\ from\ the\ diagonal\ }x=y{\rm \ assuming\ independence}}.</math>

When the concordance correlation coefficient is computed on a length-<math>N</math> data set (i.e., <math>N</math> paired values <math>(x_n, y_n)</math>, for <math>n=1,...,N</math>), the form is
:<math>\hat{\rho}_c = \frac{2 s_{xy}}{s_x^2 + s_y^2 + (\bar{x} - \bar{y})^2},</math>
where the mean is computed as
:<math>\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N x_n</math>
and the variance
:<math>s_x^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N (x_n - \bar{x})^2</math>
and the covariance
:<math>s_{xy} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N (x_n - \bar{x})(y_n - \bar{y}) .</math>

Whereas the ordinary [[Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient|correlation coefficient]] (Pearson's) is immune to whether the biased or unbiased versions for estimation of the variance is used, the concordance correlation coefficient is not. In the original article, Lin suggested normalizing with <math>1/N</math> normalization,<ref name="LinL1989Concordance"/>
while in another article Nickerson appears to have used <math>1/(N-1)</math>,<ref name="NickersonC1997Note">{{Cite journal
 | author = Carol A. E. Nickerson
 | author-link = Carol A. E. Nickerson
 | title = A Note on "A Concordance Correlation Coefficient to Evaluate Reproducibility
 | journal = [[Biometrics (journal)|Biometrics]]
 | volume = 53
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 1503&ndash;1507
 |date=December 1997
 | doi = 10.2307/2533516
 | jstor = 2533516
 }}</ref>
i.e., the concordance correlation coefficient may be computed slightly differently between implementations.

==Relation to other measures of correlation==
The concordance correlation coefficient is nearly identical to some of the measures called [[intra-class correlation]]s. Comparisons of the concordance correlation coefficient with an "ordinary" intraclass correlation on different data sets found only small differences between the two correlations, in one case on the third decimal.<ref name="NickersonC1997Note"/> It has also been stated<ref>{{Cite journal
 |author1=Reinhold Müller |author2=Petra Büttner | title = A critical discussion of intraclass correlation coefficients
 |journal = [[Statistics in Medicine (journal)|Statistics in Medicine]]
 |date=December 1994
 | volume = 13
 | issue = 23–24
 | pages = 2465&ndash;2476
 | pmid = 7701147
 | doi = 10.1002/sim.4780132310
}}</ref> that the ideas for concordance correlation coefficient "are quite similar to results already published by Krippendorff<ref>{{Cite journal
 | author = Klaus Krippendorff
 | title = Bivariate Agreement Coefficients for Reliability of Data
 | author-link = Klaus Krippendorff
 | editor = E. F. Borgatta
 | journal = Sociological Methodology
 | volume = 2
 | pages = 139&ndash;150
 | publisher = [[Jossey-Bass]]
 | location = [[San Francisco]]
 | year = 1970
 | doi = 10.2307/270787
| title-link = Sociological Methodology
 | jstor = 270787
 }}</ref>
in 1970".

In the original article<ref name="LinL1989Concordance"/> Lin suggested a form for multiple classes (not just 2). Over ten years later a correction to this form was issued.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | author = Lawrence I-Kuei Lin
 | title = A Note on the Concordance Correlation Coefficient
 | journal = [[Biometrics (journal)|Biometrics]]
 | volume = 56
 | pages = 324&ndash;325
 |date=March 2000
 | doi = 10.1111/j.0006-341X.2000.00324.x
| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

One example of the use of the concordance correlation coefficient is in a comparison of analysis method for [[functional magnetic resonance imaging]] brain scans.<ref>{{Cite Q | Q21012624 }}</ref>
